highlights: Emperor Hirohito formally opened the 90th Imperial Diet speaking in colloquial Japanese for the first time, submitting the government's draft revised constitution for deliberation.
The Japanese Government notified eight newly elected members of the House of Representatives, including prominent party leaders, that they were disqualified under the Purge Directive.
At the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, Chief Prosecutor Joseph B. Keenan delivered opening arguments, and defendant Yosuke Matsuoka died of tuberculosis.
To alleviate desperate urban starvation, SCAP authorized the emergency distribution of 47,807 long tons of imported cereals and U.S. Army excess food stocks.
The first postwar shipments of American raw cotton arrived in Japan, initiating the processing and manufacture of cotton goods for export.
SCAP ordered the dissolution of the Japan Lumber Company and local lumber monopolies, restoring distribution functions to voluntary democratic associations.
Strict quarantine measures and naval patrols were instituted to contain a 25-case cholera outbreak on Tsushima traced to illicit shipping from Korea.

sections.title: Front matter

sections.summary: Monthly summary of political, economic, and social developments in Japan for June 1946.
sections.title: Part I: General

sections.summary: SCAP reported no changes in its non-military organization during June 1946.
sections.title: Organization Under SCAP

sections.summary: The 90th Imperial Diet opened with the Emperor speaking in colloquial Japanese and receiving the draft constitution. SCAP conferred with 31 women Diet members, eight Diet members were purged, and the Demobilization Board was created under Shidehara.
sections.title: Political Activities

sections.summary: SCAP extended authorized fishing grounds, while coal and lumber production remained below target. The first shipment of American raw cotton arrived, staple food reserves fell to 45.3 days, and currency circulation reached ¥40,644,000,000.
sections.title: Economic Activities

sections.summary: Public relief assisted 2,182,662 individuals, and cumulative Japanese repatriates reached 3,685,378. Teacher screening began in Chiba Prefecture, the Ministry of Education published the new Teachers' Manual, and cholera outbreaks in Kyushu were quarantined.
sections.title: Social Activities

sections.summary: Covers Japanese government administration, political parties, Diet proceedings, public safety, and war crimes trials.
sections.title: Part II: Political

sections.summary: The 90th Diet convened as the Emperor submitted the draft constitution and Prime Minister Yoshida outlined government policies. Eight Diet members and several peers were purged, the Demobilization Board was established, and the Emperor toured Chiba and Shizuoka.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Mass demonstrations subsided following SCAP warnings, police raided Tokyo's Ueno black market, and crackdowns targeted lethal bootleg liquor. Recommendations were submitted for police decentralization, while prison death rates remained critically elevated.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: Military occupation courts heard 1,550 cases, and SCAP ordered the arrest of 56 war crime suspects. At the IMTFE, Chief Prosecutor Keenan presented opening statements, key witnesses testified on Japanese militarism, and defendant Yosuke Matsuoka died.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: Covers natural resources, industry, commerce, labor, finance, trade, and reparations.
sections.title: Part III: Economic

sections.summary: A reconnaissance soil survey of Kyushu was completed, and SCAP doubled authorized offshore fishing and whaling areas. Hokkaido herring catches reached 207,947 metric tons, while live ko-ayu fry were transplanted from Lake Biwa to nationwide streams.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: SCAP ordered dissolution of the monopolistic Japan Lumber Company. May coal output reached 1,695,000 metric tons, failing minimum quotas due to food shortages, while a newly formed petroleum committee estimated national reserves at 10,000,000 kiloliters.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: Production gains occurred in pig iron, steel, aluminum, and cement, but severe coal shortages restricted metal refining and chemical output. Commercial nitrogenous fertilizer production reached half of prewar peak levels, and 250 merchant vessels were repaired.
sections.title: Heavy Industries

sections.summary: Canned fish and flour milling production increased, but shortages of fuel and containers constrained food processing. Output rose for paper, sheet glass, and bicycles, while 1,272 truck chassis and expanding supplies of farm implements were manufactured.
sections.title: Manufacturing

sections.summary: The first post-war American raw cotton arrived for processing, boosting cotton cloth weaving by 50 percent for export. Raw silk production rose to 7,540 bales, rayon pulp manufacturing resumed, and silk fabric output more than doubled.
sections.title: Textile Industries

sections.summary: Rail freight increased to 8,527,200 metric tons and rolling stock additions improved operations, while coastal shipping declined slightly. Hydroelectric generation supplied ample electric power, but 70 percent of municipal gas capacity remained idle for lack of coal.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: An Imperial ordinance elevated the Board of Communications to a Ministry effective 1 July. Higher domestic postal and telephone rates were introduced, radio receiver production jumped 40 percent, and the 400,000-member All Japan Communications Workers' Union was inaugurated.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: The Cabinet approved the Labor Disputes Adjustment Bill, and registered union membership reached 2,695,988 across 7,207 unions. The April census revealed 5,600,000 totally or partially unemployed persons, and plans were made to establish a separate Ministry of Labor.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: Arrival of 21,712 bales of American raw cotton initiated Japan's textile export-import program. June exports included 11,053 bales of raw silk and 70,000 metric tons of coal, while imports provided 60,000 tons of food grains and Chinese wheat bran.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: Critical urban food deficits required emergency SCAP releases of 47,807 long tons of imported cereals and flour. New official vegetable ceilings eliminated subsidies, rubber goods prices were adjusted upward, and economic police recorded 144,353 rationing and price violations.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Bank of Japan note issue reached ¥40,644,000,000, though the daily expansion rate slowed. The government operated under temporary budget authorizations and short-term loans, local tax reforms were enacted to raise ¥3,327,000,000, and national debt reached ¥203,064,000,000.
sections.title: Finance

sections.summary: SCAP impounded properties of 10 zaibatsu families, placed four second-line holding companies under surveillance, and added 17 holding companies to the restricted schedule. Custody was reported over 594 potential reparations facilities and ¥63,024,347 in war criminal assets.
sections.title: Property Control and Reparations

sections.summary: Covers public health, welfare, repatriation, education, religion, arts, monuments, and media of expression.
sections.title: Part IV: Social

sections.summary: Welfare relief assisted 2,182,493 individuals, while repatriates returned to Japan reached 3,685,378. Rigorous port quarantines and sanitary cordons contained cholera outbreaks in Tsushima and Kyushu, 16,000,000 people were revaccinated against smallpox, and DDT duster production expanded.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: Teacher screening was launched in Chiba Prefecture, the Ministry of Education distributed the new democratic Teachers' Manual, and Imperial portrait depositories were removed from schools. The Tokyo war crimes trials and Diet constitution debates dominated public media.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

summary: Summation No. 9 covers non-military activities across occupied Japan during June 1946, highlighting political democratization, acute economic distress, and critical public health interventions. Politically, the 90th Imperial Diet opened under the new Yoshida Cabinet, with Emperor Hirohito delivering an unprecedented opening address in colloquial Japanese and formally submitting the draft revised constitution. SCAP and the Japanese government intensified the political purge, disqualifying prominent Diet members, while the International Military Tribunal for the Far East commenced its substantive prosecution phase. Economically, Japan faced a severe food crisis characterized by depleted urban rice stocks and widespread absenteeism, prompting emergency SCAP releases of 47,807 long tons of imported food. Industrial recovery was inaugurated by the arrival of the first postwar shipments of American raw cotton, even as critical shortages of coal and raw materials hindered heavy manufacturing. Meanwhile, union membership expanded to 2.7 million workers, and major holding company properties were impounded. Socially, authorities contained cholera outbreaks in Kyushu through strict maritime quarantine and launched nationwide teacher screening. For historians, the report provides invaluable data on constitutional deliberations, labor unrest, zaibatsu dissolution, and food relief logistics.
